medical examiner’s office also visited the scene and spoke to an FBI agent, who said the agency “would be taking jurisdiction of the case,” according to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/11/17/silverio-villegas-gonzalez-ice-dhs-trump-midway-blitz-shooting-homicide-franklin-park-chicago" target="_blank" >an autopsy report</a>.</p><p>Witz handed emergency radio recordings over to the FBI days later, emails show. He<b> </b>also<b> </b>acknowledged<b> </b>having<b> </b>“numerous phone conversations and face to face conversation[s] with FBI and [Homeland Security Investigations] agents.”</p><p>The FBI says a U.S. Department of Justice policy prevents them from “commenting on the nature of any investigations that may or may not be occurring.”</p><p>Lawyers for Villegas González’s family believe the FBI closed its case in mid-October when they returned his car and personal belongings to relatives.</p><p>By April, Franklin Park asked a state police task force to conduct an investigation of the shooting — the same day the Illinois Accountability Commission released a damning report detailing the actions of federal agents during Midway Blitz. The commission concluded that “federal agents shot and killed Villegas González without apparent justification.”</p><p>In the request to ISP, Franklin Park police indicated the department didn’t have any evidence logs, use-of-force reports or photos from the scene.</p><p>The ISP investigation is still open, according to an agency spokesperson. It will likely culminate in a referral to Cook County State’s Attorney Eileen O’Neill Burke, who would have to determine whether to bring charges.</p><p>The state’s attorney’s office has been “actively supporting” the ISP investigation, and similar probes led by Chicago police, O'Neill Burke says.</p><p>Her office has developed the state’s first protocol for use-of-force incidents involving on-duty federal agents. In July, it launched a working group to analyze “complex legal and evidentiary issues” that could arise from such cases, O'Neill Burke says.</p><p>“When we receive one, we will conduct a thorough review and will not hesitate to prosecute if the facts and the law support charges,” O'Neill Burke says.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-200001" name="image-200001"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/da80eed/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6000x3367+0+0/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F56%2F0a%2F0e5ac6134b85b9d0775687301c2f%2Fspecialprosecutor-260522-9.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/988b8c9/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6000x3367+0+0/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F56%2F0a%2F0e5ac6134b85b9d0775687301c2f%2Fspecialprosecutor-260522-9.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/307dc69/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6000x3367+0+0/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F56%2F0a%2F0e5ac6134b85b9d0775687301c2f%2Fspecialprosecutor-260522-9.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Cook County State’s Attorney Eileen O’Neill Burke speaks after a hearing at the George N. class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Cook County State’s Attorney Eileen O’Neill Burke speaks to reporters at the Leighton Criminal Courthouse in May after a judge rejected a push to appoint a special prosecutor to investigate Operation Midway Blitz.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>A key legal question for prosecutors could be whether the agents who confronted Villegas González acted reasonably in the course of their duties.</p><p>DHS previously told the Sun-Times in July that the U.S. attorney’s office had <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/07/22/mexico-seeks-accountability-in-chicago-area-ice-death-and-16-others-can-it-force-the-u-s-to-act" target="_blank" >declined to prosecute</a> the ICE agent who shot Villegas González. The feds haven’t publicly explained why.</p><p>Meantime, Mexico has also sought answers.</p><p>Officials for the country <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/07/22/mexico-seeks-accountability-in-chicago-area-ice-death-and-16-others-can-it-force-the-u-s-to-act" target="_blank" >called for an investigation</a> and sent a diplomatic note to the U.S. government, according to Reyna Torres Mendívil, Mexico’s consul general in Chicago. There had been no official response by July. Mexico later called for investigations into the deaths of 17 Mexican nationals that were linked to immigration enforcement, including Villegas González’s.</p><p>The officials say that Mexico continues to assist Villegas González’s family in a child custody case and is closely following the legal proceedings.</p><h3><b>‘Silverio was killed twice’</b></h3><p>Community members, immigrant rights organizers and faith leaders have spent the past year trying to keep Villegas González’s name alive.</p><p>Marien Casillas Pabellón, executive director of PASO - West Suburban Action Project, is helping organize a march Saturday to mark the anniversary of Villegas González’s death and renew calls for transparency.</p><p>“Part of our march Saturday is to make sure he isn’t forgotten,” Casillas Pabellón says.</p><p>She remembers the confusion in Franklin Park as local and federal law enforcement responded to the shooting.</p><p>Children were placed under lockdown inside a nearby school as parents tried to figure out what was happening. By the time Casillas Pabellón arrived, Villegas González had been taken away. She remembers his car, and the blood on the pavement.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-d70000" name="image-d70000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/92c1be1/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F09%2F7b%2Fddb8852b4cd38affc5a9acd9ec4a%2Fwatchsilverio-2609130167.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/363217e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F09%2F7b%2Fddb8852b4cd38affc5a9acd9ec4a%2Fwatchsilverio-2609130167.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/f6675c7/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F09%2F7b%2Fddb8852b4cd38affc5a9acd9ec4a%2Fwatchsilverio-2609130167.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Marien Casillas Pabellon, executive director of PASO, poses in front of a memorial near the site of the shooting of Silverio Villegas González in Chicago on September 10, 2026. They organized a news conference, and someone brought candles and flowers to the corner where Villegas González had been shot.</p><p>Members of Hijas del Pueblo, a grassroots group of women and neighbors from Franklin Park and surrounding communities, continued tending to the site, maintaining the flowers and turning the corner into a place of remembrance and community.</p><p>A year later, residents have successfully pushed Franklin Park for a permanent memorial to Villegas González.</p><p>Casillas Pabellón says he was “killed twice.”</p><p>“They killed him that day during the traffic stop,” she says, “and they killed him again with all the lies they told about him afterward.”</p><p>She notes that Villegas González’s death received far less national attention than later shootings by federal immigration agents. She questions whether race played a role in the disparity.</p><p>Casillas Pabellón wants people to know the person behind the headlines: a father who was responsible for his children and continued working and providing for his family despite his own health problems. “So we continue making sure that his story is known,” she says.</p><p>The Rev. Brendan Curran was among the faith leaders who got involved after Villegas González was killed. entries.title: Mayor Daley's argument that he shuttered Meigs Field out of post-9/11 security concerns never seemed credible
entries.summary: <p>As concert-goers stream onto Northerly Island this weekend to catch a show by the South Side’s own Chief Keef at an outdoor theater, they may not realize there used to be a different type of buzz there: Of planes taking off and landing at a little airport called Meigs Field.</p><p>But Chicagoans of a certain age may recall its controversy: The general aviation airfield, with a single runway and a stubby control tower, occupied the artificial island starting in the late 1940s, ultimately catering to aviation enthusiasts, along with business and government types gaining easy access — via jets, prop planes and choppers — to the Loop.</p><p>At least until 2003.</p><p>That’s when Chicago’s then-mayor, Richard M. Daley, abruptly closed the airfield by quietly ordering in heavy machinery to carve giant X marks in the 3,900-foot-long runway, rendering the site inoperable. There was no advance notice, except perhaps a backdoor tip off to select powerbrokers.</p><p>Daley explained that it was a post-9/11 security measure, with the airfield in the midst of all those high-rises, and he insisted he couldn’t jeopardize Chicago’s safety and security — though the explanation was never quite credible.</p><p>He’d wanted for years — well before 9/11 — to convert the plot into open green space, only to face resistance from flying advocates, businesspeople and state officials including then-Gov. George Ryan.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-bf0000" name="image-bf0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/c07a646/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2100x1179+0+111/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fde%2F9a%2F113e43674b37ab4210186fda7775%2Fryandaley.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/947f5a0/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2100x1179+0+111/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fde%2F9a%2F113e43674b37ab4210186fda7775%2Fryandaley.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/807c9cd/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2100x1179+0+111/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fde%2F9a%2F113e43674b37ab4210186fda7775%2Fryandaley.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Late Gov. George Ryan, at left, and ex-Mayor Richard M. Daley are shown in 2001 after reaching a deal on O'Hare Airport expansion that was supposed to keep Meigs Field open." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/807c9cd/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2100x1179+0+111/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fde%2F9a%2F113e43674b37ab4210186fda7775%2Fryandaley.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/ea66085/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2100x1179+0+111/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fde%2F9a%2F113e43674b37ab4210186fda7775%2Fryandaley.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/807c9cd/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2100x1179+0+111/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fde%2F9a%2F113e43674b37ab4210186fda7775%2Fryandaley.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Late Gov. George Ryan, at left, and ex-Mayor Richard M. Daley are shown in 2001 after reaching a deal on O’Hare Airport expansion that was supposed to keep Meigs Field open.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>AP</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>As <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/chicago/2023/03/27/meigs-field-20-years-since-daley-ordered-bulldozing" target="_blank" >WBEZ has reported</a>, Daley, a Democrat, was battling Ryan, a Republican, over Meigs’ future, and “they reached an agreement to keep Meigs open for 25 years. In exchange, Ryan supported a proposed O’Hare Airport expansion,” something Daley desired, as city officials controlled O’Hare and badly wanted runways reconfigured to remain an economic force.</p><p>But “no O’Hare bill cleared Congress, and Daley said the Meigs deal was off.”</p><p>A political nemesis of the Daley family, the late Mayor Jane Byrne, similarly proposed closing Meigs in 1980 to “make it a recreational island,” hosting “future productions of ChicagoFest,” which was a precursor to the Taste of Chicago. But that plan never materialized.</p><p>The terminal at Meigs was dedicated in 1961, when Daley’s father, the late Mayor Richard J. Daley, was in office. He was at the airfield a year earlier when then-U.S. Sen. John F. Kennedy took a helicopter to Meigs from Midway Airport while in town for what turned out to be a historic televised debate with then-Vice President Richard Nixon in the presidential race.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-fa0000" name="image-fa0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/7ad2dd1/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2100x1179+0+111/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F80%2Ffa%2Fc520f8a04883aa3b4dac8b8f9adb%2Fjack.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/faaf1b1/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2100x1179+0+111/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F80%2Ffa%2Fc520f8a04883aa3b4dac8b8f9adb%2Fjack.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/86fa5e0/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2100x1179+0+111/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F80%2Ffa%2Fc520f8a04883aa3b4dac8b8f9adb%2Fjack.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Future president John F. The Star Wars actor once slammed Daley’s closure as “an incredibly dumb thing to do,” according to a published account.</p><p>Among the crews brought in by the Daley administration to handle the Meigs destruction was Rossi Contractors, Inc., of Northlake, which remains a major O’Hare contractor and that’s been paid hundreds of millions of dollars over the years by City Hall.</p><p>The contracting entries.title: Restoring small-town charm in Roanoke, Indiana
entries.summary: <p><i>Regenerative tourism harnesses the power of sustainable travel to transform places and communities for the better. In this series, we look at Midwestern towns and small cities that have leaned into tourism to help lift local economies and create destinations that travelers want to visit.</i></p><p>Tiny Roanoke, about 10 miles south of Fort Wayne, makes a disarming first impression. Flower baskets and American flags hang from street lamps in front of restored buildings along a handsome 19th-century main street. Clothing boutiques and galleries fill refurbished storefronts interspersed with cafes and restaurants. Occasionally, elementary school students practice “plein air” painting downtown.</p><p>“I can drive my golf cart anywhere I want,” says Lee Ann Smith, the treasurer of the Roanoke Fall Festival and a 10-year town resident who moved to Roanoke when she fell “madly in love with the small-town feel.”</p><p>It wasn’t always so Mayberry. On the hunting grounds of Miami Indians, Roanoke flourished with the construction of the 468-mile Wabash & Erie Canal, which connected Toledo, Ohio to Evansville in the mid-1800s. A lock on the canal at Roanoke brought trade and traffic to town. It was later supplanted by the railroad. Eventually, Roanoke began to decline after World War II, losing its Main Street appeal to suburbs and shopping malls. By the 1980s, its retail core was largely abandoned.</p><h3>A renaissance in rural Indiana </h3><p>In 1990, Pete Eshelman, a former Yankees pitcher then working in Fort Wayne, chose tiny Roanoke to open a sports and entertainment insurance company called American Specialty. He began buying old buildings downtown and eventually opened the fine-dining restaurant <a class="Link" href="https://josephdecuis.com/" target="_blank" ><u>Joseph Decuis</u></a> (191 N. Main St.) specializing in wagyu beef that he and his family raised on their farm outside of town.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Joseph Decuis Emporium, at 151 N. Main St., makes an excellent wagyu burger. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Provided </p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“‘Our corporate life and the renaissance of Roanoke are inextricably intertwined,” wrote Eshelman in a book he co-authored, “Roanoke, The Renaissance of a Hoosier Village.”</p><p>Though local favorites like the <a class="Link" href="https://roanokevillageinn.com/" target="_blank" ><u>Roanoke Village Inn</u></a> (190 N. Main St.), which dates to 1946, predated Joseph Decuis, the Eshelmans seeded the Roanoke’s incarnation as a foodie stronghold in rural Indiana, eventually opening the more casual Joseph Decuis Emporium (151 N. Main St.). “They have excellent gumbo and wagyu burgers, which are not things you can usually get in small town restaurants,” says John Nelson, a financial advisor and the board president of the Roanoke Beautification Foundation.</p><p>Other openings followed, adding diversity. <a class="Link" href="https://thecopperstillroanoke.com/" target="_blank" ><u>The Copper Still</u></a> (165 S. Main St.) specializes in bourbon, whiskey and cocktails served alongside a robust menu of salads, sandwiches and entrees. Play dates meet up at the <a class="Link" href="https://theparkergracetearoom.com/" target="_blank" ><u>Parker Grace Tea Room</u></a> (138 W. First St.) tucked in a Victorian home for its vintage décor, light bites and desserts.</p><p>Between bites, Roanoke visitors can stop into its history museum or browse its many boutiques – among them <a class="Link" href="https://savinggracevintage.org/" target="_blank" ><u>Saving Grace Vintage</u></a> (212 N. Main St.) for furnishings, <a class="Link" href="https://ashivelyandco.com/" target="_blank" ><u>A. Shively & Co.</u></a> (138 W. First St.) for housewares with an organic bent and <a class="Link" href="https://www.roanokeoutdoordistrict.com/" target="_blank" ><u>Outdoor District</u></a> (159 N. Main St.) for men’s and women’s gear – that have helped make Roanoke a popular destination.</p><p>Nelson’s Roanoke Beautification Foundation designed Zent Commons on Main, an urban plaza with a fire pit inspired by ski resorts as a place to gather. He calls the town “borderline Norman Rockwell” and credits the all-hands approach of supportive residents. “If someone has an idea and checks the boxes and gets permission from the right entities, you can pretty much do any kind of event here you want,” he says.</p><p><b>Other things to do:</b><br>Through crash and recovery, the <a class="Link" href="https://www.roanokefallfestival.org/" target="_blank" ><u>Roanoke Fall Festival</u></a> has celebrated all things autumn. Now in its 72nd year, the weekend event, Sept. 10-12, features parades, a tractor pull, craft vendors, pie and ice cream eating contests, a baked goods competition, pig races and a rodeo as well as food and music.</p><p>Outside of town, parks are big attractions in surrounding Huntington County, including the recently expanded <a class="Link" href="https://www.in.gov/dnr/state-parks/parks-lakes/salamonie-lake/" target="_blank" ><u>Salamonie Lake State Park</u></a> protecting the namesake reservoir and surroundings popular with hikers and fishermen. <a class="Link" href="https://www.rusticriveroutfitters.com/" target="_blank" ><u>Rustic Rivers Outfitters</u></a> in the village of Mt. Etna offers canoe and kayak trips on the Salamonie and Wabash Rivers (6062 W. 600 S., Huntington). Thrill-seekers can ride eight zip lines and traverse four aerial bridges at <a class="Link" href="http://www.discovertimberlake.com/" target="_blank" ><u>Camp Timber Lake</u></a> about five miles south of Roanoke (1740 E. 675 N., Huntington). Don’t miss the <a class="Link" href="https://www.huntington.in.us/egov/apps/locations/facilities.egov?view=detail&id=50" target="_blank" ><u>Sunken Gardens</u></a> in Huntington created of an abandoned quarry (1125 W. Park Dr., Huntington).</p><p>Near Camp Timber Lake, <a class="Link" href="https://twoees.com/" target="_blank" ><u>Two-EE’s Winery</u></a> offers glasses, flights, tastings, slushies and bottles of its estate-grown wines (6808 N. US Highway 24, Huntington). A dog-friendly outdoor patio and lawn host concerts, outdoor movies and trivia nights.</p><p><b>Where to stay:</b><br>Live like a townie in a downtown <a class="Link" href="https://www.airbnb.com/rooms/54115722?search_mode=regular_search&adults=1&check_in=2026-08-22&check_out=2026-08-27&children=0&infants=0&pets=0&source_impression_id=p3_1787179455_P3BYDwhIuLInJC0y&previous_page_section_name=1000&federated_search_id=6f71a2be-8de2-4e7c-96c8-3ab4a890f686" target="_blank" ><u>home on Airbnb</u></a>. Just north of Roanoke, the <a class="Link" href="https://josephdecuis.com/farmstead" target="_blank" ><u>Joseph Decuis Farmstead Inn</u></a> (6756 E. 900 S., Columbia City) offers six bedrooms in restored 1884 farm buildings including a farmhouse, carriage house and barn.</p>

entries.title: Chicago Fire Department commemorates the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks
entries.summary: <p>Chicagoans woke to a clear blue sky and a light fall breeze Friday, just as they did 25 years ago. At Navy Pier, Chicago Fire Department members stood at attention for a memorial ceremony to commemorate the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks. Many of the firefighters in attendance were too young to remember that day; others in attendance had caravanned in 2001 to New York City to help firefighters search through the rubble of the Twin Towers.</p><p>Dignitaries including Sen. Dick Durbin, Gov. JB Pritzker, Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson and Illinois Reps. Jonathan Jackson, Delia Ramirez and Mike Quigley stood by but did not speak to the crowd.</p><p>Instead, a CFD chaplain offered a prayer for the departed as Chicago Fire boats floated off the pier and a CFD helicopter soared over the crowd. Bagpipers played “Amazing Grace” followed by an Illinois State Police trooper playing “Taps.”</p><p>The ceremony was a short and solemn reminder of another beautiful September day.</p><div entries.title: 25 years after 9/11, Chicagoans reflect on how that day changed their lives
entries.summary: <p>Dion McGill had been in the Illinois Army National Guard for just 11 months when America was attacked on Sept. 11, 2001. </p><p>The morning after his 22nd birthday, McGill's sister alerted him to the news.</p><p>McGill, who lives in Englewood and is now 41, had taken that day off. They turned on the TV and saw news broadcasts just before watching a second plane hit the World Trade Center towers in New York City. </p><p>There were later reports that a third plane struck the Pentagon and another crashed into a field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania.</p><p>“You could feel the seismic shift almost immediately,” he said. “Obviously, the world is different. You just don't know how different.”</p><p>McGill had signed up for the Guard for tuition assistance after running out of money while a student at Western Illinois University before eventually dropping out.</p><p>“I thought I would fill sandbags if there was flooding, maybe help a lady or two across the street,” he said.</p><p>McGill completed basic training shortly before 9/11, but his advanced individual training — which teaches recruits the specifics of their jobs — was delayed by nearly two years.</p><p>The job he chose came with an $8,000 signing bonus, specializing in mitigating deaths in the event of any nuclear, biological or chemical attacks.</p><h3>Sense of duty</h3><p>In 2004, three years after 9/11, McGill’s unit was preparing for deployment to Iraq as part of a U.S. military operation in the region when they were diverted to Germany days before their scheduled departure.</p><p>“A lot of soldiers were being killed,” McGill said, explaining that troops already familiar with the region were being sent to Iraq while soldiers less familiar with the area were diverted elsewhere.</p><p>McGill recalled feeling relieved he could support the war without heading to Iraq. He would spend 15 months in Germany.</p><p>But, in 2008, his unit was later deployed to Afghanistan. McGill said he returned home with a fractured hip, a bad back, post-traumatic stress disorder, nasal polyps, sleep apnea and “a host of stories and memories I could have easily done without in this life.”</p><p>He finally got his degree from Saint Xavier University in 2010, but several friends never made it home. He wonders about the lives they could have gone on to have lived.</p><p>“One thing my mind always wraps around is this idea that Josh will forever be 21. Jason will always be this mid-20s guy,” he said of his friends Josh Harris and Jason Vasquez.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Dion McGill, now 41, signed up to serve in the Illinois Army National Guard 11 months before 9/11. He said the event and experiences in the military left him with a sense of duty. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Provided </p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>McGill said the experiences left him with a new fearlessness and resolve.</p><p>“I came home with a sense of duty that has permeated the fabric of my life ever since,” he said, pointing to his current work as a counselor in Englewood.</p><p>McGill said he  receives disability pay for his PTSD and has found therapy helpful, but the survivor's guilt hasn’t left him.</p><p>“You fall into that rabbit hole of guilt and sorrow, and that's not how I want to honor their memories,” he said.</p><h3>‘I wish we could have done more’</h3><p>Days before the 25th anniversary of 9/11, New York City released more than <u>170,000 pages</u> of records concerning post-9/11 air quality and the city’s response.</p><p>For <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2021/9/10/22665003/sept11-chicago-cops-firefighters-new-york-911" target="_blank" ><u>Jim and Pat Maloney</u></a>, Chicago brothers who rushed to help at Ground Zero after the attacks, the records have renewed questions about the air quality first responders were exposed to.</p><p>Jim Maloney, 72, a retired Chicago Police Department lieutenant who was a cop for more than 35 years, said he never had asthma before 9/11. Since then, he's developed a cough that now requires an inhaler to control. </p><p>Maloney and his brother are among the thousands enrolled in the World Trade Center Health program.</p><p>Pat Maloney, 65, a retired Chicago Fire Department battalion chief, was treated for cancer. </p><p>As a firefighter for more than 40 years, he says the concerns about the air quality don't change his views about having gone to New York to do what he could in 2001.</p><p>“It's not about self-preservation,” Maloney said in an interview while in New York, where he traveled to mark the 25th anniversary of the attacks. “We show up at a scene that's very dangerous and hazardous, and we gotta put calm to some chaos.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> Englewood sculpture park brings hope for ‘good things’</a></h3><p></p><h5>Reporting by <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydsjuut-l-il/" target="_blank" >Courtney Kueppers</a></h5><p>On a recent weekday morning, there was a buzz of activity along Englewood's 63rd Street between May Street and Racine Avenue. The corner brimmed with oversized drum sculptures and colorful murals.</p><p>It was all part of a new sculpture park, courtesy of the artist-driven Englewood Arts Collective. The group soft-launched the public art installation in August and will host activities here this weekend in alignment with the annual Englewood Music Festival.</p><p>Over the next three to five years, the collective plans to fill this once-vacant lot with art and give neighbors a place of beauty to gather.</p><p>The sculpture park is the latest initiative since the collective — made up of 10 artists — launched nearly a decade ago. Collective members say art has always had a home in Englewood. That includes the longstanding Englewood Jazz Festival, which will take place Sept. 17-19.</p><p>"Artistic acts like this and creative spaces like this can catalytically support other well-being initiatives," said collective co-founder Janell Nelson. "Positive foot traffic to this corridor can help the economic outcomes of the other businesses in this corridor, and it’s been proven."</p><p><b>Three free things to do in Englewood this month</b>:</p><ul class="rte2-style-ul" style="line-height: inherit; margin-top: 20px; margin-bottom: 20px; margin-left: 24px; padding: 0px; list-style-type: disc;" id="rte-1ad69280-ade2-11f1-b59f-edede58e0cca"><li><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydsjuut-l-ir/" target="_blank" ><b>Englewood Music Festival</b></a>: Saturday at Kennedy King College, West 64th Street & South Halsted Street<br> </li><li><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydsjuut-l-iy/" target="_blank" ><b>EAC Arts Village Sculpture Park</b></a>:<a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydsjuut-l-ij/" target="_blank" > </a>Ongoing at West 63rd Street, between May Street and Racine Avenue<br> </li><li><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydsjuut-l-it/" target="_blank" ><b>Englewood Jazz Festival</b></a>: Sept. 17-19 at Hamilton Park, 513 W. 72nd St.<br></li></ul><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydsjuut-l-ii/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>YOUR DAILY QUESTION ☕️</h4><h4></h4><p><b>How would you reimagine public transportation in Chicago?</b></p><p><a class="Link" href="mailto:newsletters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" ><i>Reply to this question via email</i></a><i> (please include your first and last name). entries.title: 5 things to know about lawyer-turned-influencer Rachel Cohen, Brandon Johnson's new chief spokesperson
entries.summary: <p>A Harvard-trained attorney turned activist and influencer who gained notoriety protesting Operation Midway Blitz and boycotting her federal income taxes is being tapped to lead Mayor Brandon Johnson’s communications office.</p><p></p><p>Here’s what you need to know about Rachel Cohen, 32, who is now tasked with telling Johnson’s story at a time when he’s expected to embark on a tough battle for reelection.</p><h3><b>Who is Rachel Cohen? </b></h3><p>Cohen is a Harvard-trained attorney from Ohio. She taught English literature to non-English speakers in Rhode Island before deciding to go to law school.</p><p>Cohen first went viral in March 2025 when she publicly resigned from the law firm Skadden, Arps, Slate, Meagher & Flom LLP, accusing the firm of capitulating to the Trump administration when it was waging war on corporate law firms. The firm cut a deal with President Donald Trump to provide $100 million in pro bono work to avoid a series of executive orders. Before leaving, Cohen worked on financing for large corporations and private equity acquisitions.</p><p>Since then, Cohen has turned to activism. She was arrested for civil disobedience at the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) processing office in Broadview that was being used as a detention facility during the height of Operation Midway Blitz. She was hit with tear gas or pepper bullets half a dozen times during those protests, she said.</p><p>Cohen also gained notoriety for refusing to pay her federal income taxes out of protest. At the time, most of her income was from freelance work.</p><p>“I was thinking about my willingness to be hit with chemical weapons,” <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/04/24/tax-protest-civil-disobedience-tax-avoidance-trump-israel-iran-gaza" >Cohen told WBEZ in April.</a> “And I couldn’t square giving the federal government $10,000.”</p><p>She said she will now need to pay federal taxes as a government employee, but that she is not currently planning to pay the $10,000 she owes from her freelance work.</p><h3><b>What is Cohen’s national reach? </b></h3><p>Cohen has 290,000 followers on Instagram and 363,000 on TikTok. Her videos on progressive politics regularly get tens of thousands of likes and hundreds or thousands of comments. Cohen is also engaged in the progressive, anti-establishment movement outside of Illinois. She did outreach for winning Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan.</p><h3><b>Why did Johnson hire Cohen? </b></h3><p>Cohen’s hiring marks another sign that Johnson wants to communicate more directly with constituents and voters as he has struggled to convey his wins in traditional media.</p><p>“The way people get their news and information is changing, and we have to meet Chicagoans where they are,” Johnson said in a statement. “Rachel understands how to take complex issues and make them accessible, while bringing the work of this administration directly to people on every platform.”</p><p>Johnson has been leaning on paid influencers who provide favorable analysis and share hand-picked messaging in recent months. Cohen has interviewed Johnson multiple times in short social media videos, but declined to take payment from the administration.</p><p>Cohen recently did an explainer on the political influence of businessman Michael Sacks, claiming “Michael Sacks wants to buy all of your elections.” Sacks, a close advisor to former Mayor Rahm Emanuel, has donated roughly $1.4 million to Common Ground Collective, a group involved in school board elections that also ran commercials poking holes in Johnson’s revenue plans for his failed corporate head tax proposal. He also gave $500,000 to mayoral contender Alexi Giannoulias.</p><p>The video is meant to boost awareness of a major political player in the city, Cohen said. But it has also prompted some threatening comments such as “He should be scared.” Cohen said she was unaware of the comments and denounces calls for violence. She has a blanket policy of not moderating comments on viral videos, she said, which would be “untenable.”</p><p>“I do not condone comments that are calling for violence against anyone… including business leaders in our community,” she said.</p><h3><b>What does Cohen want to accomplish in the role? </b></h3><p>Cohen argued there is a misunderstanding of “how much of a progressive champion Mayor Johnson is” and that her goal will be to communicate that message.</p><p>“It's unfathomable to me because he is objectively one of the most progressive mayors in the country and was probably the most progressive mayor in the country when he was elected back in 2023,” Cohen said.</p><p>Cohen does not have any traditional communications experience in politics, though she emphasized her respect for legacy news outlets and often shares local reporting. She said Friday her hiring doesn’t mean a de-prioritization of trained journalists over social media influencers.</p><p>“We're going to see an emphasis broadly on meeting people where they are, and for many people that is traditional press,” Cohen said. “For many people, that is new media. What we're going to be focused on is sharing the many wins and investments that Mayor Johnson has made in our communities with people in as many formats as possible, and in language that is easy to understand.”</p><h3><b>Who does Cohen replace? </b></h3><p>Cohen replaces Communications Director Erin Connelly. Cohen’s first day is Monday.</p><p>Connelly currently makes $200,856 in her role, according to the city’s employee database. She took the permanent position after the ouster of Ronnie Reese in the fall of 2024. Reese, a longtime ally of Johnson’s who worked at the Chicago Teachers Union, left amid harassment and bullying allegations.</p><p>Others who came and went include Joe Calvello, who took on the role of “chief strategy officer” after working for U.S. Sen. John Fetterman, a Pennsylvania Democrat. Calvello now works for New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. So does Cassio Mendoza, who worked previously as a press secretary for Johnson.</p><p><i>Contributing: City Hall reporter Fran Spielman</i></p>

entries.title: Chief Keef to kick off his headlining tour in Chicago
entries.summary: <p>On the second night of Ye’s star-studded homecoming concert Sept. 5 at Soldier Field, Yeezy brought an unexpected special guest. In his first concert appearance within city limits in more than a decade, <a class="Link" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3Pa2oRsrewE" target="_blank" ><u>Chief Keef</u></a> rose atop the gigantic electronic globe under angry red lights to the shock of the sold-out stadium.</p><p>As if he were the drill Michael Jackson himself, the whole stadium erupted as Keef stood for a few seconds and gave Ye a dap. “Chief Sosa in the f------ building, yes sir,” he said before he performed his 2012 hit, “Love Sosa.” It was a historic moment for the once-maligned rapper/producer/entrepreneur that no one, not even him, could have imagined.</p><p>“I didn’t think I would make it as far as Soldier Field,” said Keef earlier this month in a phone interview from his home in Los Angeles. “It’s a good feeling to be able to do stuff like that. And then the stage is crazy; I’ve never been on a stage like that before. That was kind of cool, bro, to be with all the ‘Chiraq’ legends.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times file</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The guest appearance at Ye’s concert was a warm-up to the “Chief Keef Live 2026” tour kickoff concert on Saturday at Huntington Bank Pavilion at Northerly Island. Now 31, the South Side native, born Keith Cozart, is kicking the tour off in his hometown because, after years of returning for his peers, he says it’s time for him to have his own homecoming. (<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/music/2024/06/13/chief-keef-long-road-back-to-chicago-for-summer-smash-industry-insiders-weigh-in" target="_blank" ><u>Keef performed in Bridgeview in 2024</u></a> and this year at Summer Smash but not in the city proper.)</p><p>“Because that’s the city! I’ve been back numerous times for other shows, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/music/2026/09/03/kanye-west-ye-chicago-legacy-essays" target="_blank" ><u>Kanye,</u></a> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/music/2026/06/11/cole-bennett-summer-smash-hip-hop-festivals-chicago-chief-keef-juice-wrld-eminem" target="_blank" ><u>Cole Bennett,</u></a> why not do my s---,” said Keef.</p><p>Chief Keef rose to prominence in 2011 through his viral, homemade music videos like “Bang” and “300.” As his music soundtracked the rampant gang violence in the early 2010s, his music spread from high schools to nightclubs and beyond. Then, his song “I Don’t Like” took off, leading to a short-lived deal with Interscope Records.<b> </b></p><p>Since then, Chief Keef has rebuilt his career as an independent artist with his own label, 43B, moved to Los Angeles and tried to confront the legal issues that mounted as a teen that have held him back: time under house arrest as he built his following on YouTube before breaking out and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2017/12/28/18340292/warrant-issued-for-chief-keef-s-arrest-in-california" target="_blank" ><u>multiple warrants issued for his arrest</u></a> for unpaid The rapper rose to prominence in 2011 through his viral, homemade music videos like “Bang” and “300” as a teen.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Sun-Times file</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>He was also unofficially blacklisted from Chicago venues for the better part of a decade, which is why Keef had to appear via hologram at <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2015/7/25/18559354/hammond-police-pull-plug-on-chief-keef-hologram-appearance" target="_blank" ><u>a 2015 Indiana show,</u></a> a benefit to raise money for victims of gun violence, including his friend, Martin “Capo” Carr. The office of then-mayor Rahm Emanuel released a statement calling him “an unacceptable role model” and labeled the performance “a significant public safety risk.”</p><p>By then, he had left Chicago amid what he describes as intense hostility from rival gangs and the city of Chicago under Emanuel.</p><p> “He had to get out of Chicago. He’s the father of drill music. A lot of political people and police didn’t like him,” said his uncle, Alonzo Cozart, adding that drill was frowned upon for its allusions to real crimes and gangbanging. </p><p>Keef said of that time, “I just felt like they were picking with me, that’s all, when I was trying to do good, do better. But that’s OK; that’s how it goes. I’m a young black mothaf---- from where I come from.”</p><p>The wheels began to turn for Keef’s return to the suburbs in 2024, a year after Mayor Brandon Johnson took office. Compared to the Emanuel administration, Johnson’s regime took an open-arms approach to working with Chicago hip-hop artists, according to longtime manager Idris “Peeda Pan” Abdul-Wahid.</p><p>“Once Mayor Johnson, once he got in, that provided us the opportunity to really have a sit-down with someone that we knew would hear things out and try to work with us in whatever way we needed and have certain safeguards in place,” Abdul-Wahid said. Crisis manager Cheo Patrick, Abdul-Wahid’s adviser Marc Whitaker and his son Marc Whitaker II worked with Johnson’s senior adviser Jason Lee to <a class="Link" href="https://www.complex.com/music/a/complex/chief-keef-performed-in-chicago-for-the-first-time-in-over" target="_blank" ><u>clear the legal path </u></a>for Keef's return home.</p><p>Living in Los Angeles was an aspiration for Keef. The rapper said he views it as a place where people “make it.” By moving, he was able to get away from the tumultuous lifestyle in Chicago and to grow as a person, artist and businessman.</p><div data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>By moving to LA, Chief Keef says he was able to get away from the tumultuous lifestyle in Chicago and to grow as a person, artist and businessman. But he says he’s grown tired of the city and it’s time for “something new.”</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Casimir Spaulding</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“Growing up, you see L.A., you see Hollywood on TV all the time, you think that’s when you made it when you get the hell out. Especially when you’re coming up, you’re growing up in poverty. You don’t think that the same s— that’s going on in Chicago is going on in L.A.,” said Keef. “Not only did L.A help me grow, but I had a chance to get away from the s--- I was in, that’s all.”</p><p>Despite Los Angeles’s own deep history of gang culture, along with a running count of rappers being burglarized, extorted and murdered, Chief Keef has managed to steer clear of it. On top of his relentless work ethic as an artist and producer, he said he sticks to himself, doesn’t party, and stays out of the mix. He’s also been sober since 2022.</p><p>“I don’t like to mix up. I’m from a whole ‘nother place. I know certain people; I just don’t like to mix up. I’m not on all that; I respect people from afar.”</p><p>But nowadays, he says he's ready to move on from the City of Dreams.</p><p>“I’m tired of LA; one of these days, I’mma get the f--- outta here. I’ve been here for a while, and it’s time for something new,” said Keef.</p><p>But when asked if he’s ready to come back home, considering how much he especially misses Chicago’s food, his immediate response: “S--- no. Hell naw. I put in my time already.”</p><p>Keef lost many of the childhood friends and family members he started his journey with in Chicago. Along with Blood Money and his friend Capo, he lost his cousin and fellow drill pioneer Fredo Santana from a drug overdose in 2018. And right before his Summer Smash performance in 2024, his friend T-Slick was killed in Peoria.</p><p>His biggest loss came from his beloved grandmother, Margaret Louise Carter, who died in 2022. In 2005, she became his legal guardian and was with him every step of his rap career, even when she didn’t understand the music he was making at the time. In fact, she’s the first voice you hear on “Breaking Down,” the first song on his latest album, “Skeletor.”</p><p>“She was my everything. I always loved my Granny; she did a lot for me. She could have the world if I could give it to her,” he said.</p><p> Carter, a longtime bus driver, appeared in many of Keef’s music videos filmed at her house as the voice of order. In many ways, she is a muse of his music as he would sample her voice and rap about her frequently. She famously scolded Keef in a viral video of him coming from jail, yelling, “Pull your pants up; that’s what you do! That’s ugly!”</p><p>“I still do a lot of s--- that I do for her. Usually, when it’s time to do something, sometimes I might not wanna do stuff. And a lot of times I think, ‘I do it for my Granny,’” said Keef. </p><p>When asked what his grandmother would say if she saw him performing at Soldier Field and starting his major tour in Chicago after the personal tragedies and legal problems, he said she would be proud.</p><p>“She would be bragging to her sisters. She would call them up and brag; she would love that s--- for real. I would have picked her up and taken her with me,” he said.</p>

entries.title: Chicago murals: Connecting neighborhoods with viaduct art, starting with Bronzeville and Chinatown
entries.summary: <p>The new mural under the CTA Red Line viaduct at Cermak Road and South Clark Street is the first of three to encourage residents to walk between the vibrant and unique communities of Bronzeville, Chinatown and Pilsen.</p><p>The three communities of color are separated both by social and physical boundaries, say Consuela Hendricks and Angela X Lin, co-presidents and co-founders of People Matter, a nonprofit whose goal is to end racism in three to five generations.</p><p>By improving the viaducts, which often serve as geographical neighborhood boundaries, they hope to encourage residents of Bronzeville, a historically Black neighborhood; Chinatown, a historically Asian neighborhood; and Pilsen, a historically Latino neighborhood, to explore each other's communities.</p><p>“We can walk into each other’s communities and learn,” Hendricks says.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure and Latino communities. The mural project, titled Breaking Community Bubbles, aims to do just that.</p><p>The first mural was completed this summer on the Cermak Road border of Bronzeville and Chinatown on the south wall of the viaduct. It features a Black woman’s face that, on one half, is overlaid with flowers and sparkles and seems to disappear into the purple background. On the other side, the woman’s black hair gives way to sunflowers, with strings of gold sparkly paint coming down the wall along the cracks. Swirls of broken mirror pieces lead to an image of a tree draped with Spanish moss. Along the bottom, words from W.E.B. DuBois discuss the concept of double consciousness, what it means to hold identities as a Black person and an American.</p><p>A quote from Hendricks on the far left side of the mural reads, “The key to one’s own solidarity is not by one’s merit but one’s ability to act when injustice is in front of us. To not let the waves of racism, xenophobia and cowardice get in the way of freedom for ourselves and others. Let bigotry die in our generation or the next generation will inherit the burden of its sorrows.”</p><p>The title of this first mural is “Soul,” the women say.</p><div class="Enhancement" the arts.</p><p>In addition to being co-presidents and co-founders of People Matter, Hendricks and Lin were artists on the mural. Hendricks created the design and gave direction, while Lin “made a lot of it happen,” Hendricks says. More than 30 kids who participate in People Matter school programs helped paint the mural on the viaduct wall.</p><p>One of the challenges to the mural was painting on a wall and viaduct in need of repair. The entire mural is painted with acrylic paint, with pieces of mirror providing texture and reflection.</p><p>Lin said the decision to paint over the large cracks in the wall with gold sparkly paint was inspired by Kintsugi, a Japanese art technique of repairing broken pottery with a gold lacquer. Instead of throwing away something because it’s broken, the pieces are instead made more valuable.</p><p>“The infrastructure for a lot of these viaducts is falling apart. It’s probably not going to get fixed. That’s part of why people don’t want to walk through them,” Lin says. “We don’t want to ignore it. entries.title: Blackhawks prospect AJ Spellacy is tough, physical and finally close to the NHL
entries.summary: <p>Two years after <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a> forward prospect AJ Spellacy opened eyes by surviving nearly to the end of an NHL training camp, he is finally a pro player whose actual NHL debut might not be far away.</p><p>The 20-year-old Ohio native is unlikely to make the Hawks' initial roster, since there's already a slight logjam ahead of him on the contract chart and this camp isn't long enough for extended roster battles.</p><p>But if Spellacy starts the season in the AHL in Rockford, he'll have a golden opportunity to position himself first in line for a call-up, just like Nick Lardis and Oliver Moore did last season — even though he's a very different type of forward than Lardis and Moore.</p><p>It's that difference that makes Spellacy, a 2024 third-round pick, such an intriguing prospect.</p><p>He didn't put up significant point totals during his OHL junior career, so he certainly won't in the NHL, either. But he did crunch a lot of players into boards, and he has the size, strength and personality to do that in the NHL, too.</p><p>The 6-3, 205-pound former football free safety — he received a scholarship offer from Iowa State at age 16 before committing to hockey instead — is a ruthless wrecker on the ice. And he's not just tough; he's also fast, so his hits are hard to avoid.</p><p>"He's a north-south, tough-to-play-against forechecker," Rockford coach Jared Nightingale said Friday. "At this level, he'll be a penalty killer. [He'll] be a thorn in the side of the opponent, especially defensemen."</p><p>Spellacy was present for the Hawks' first official team-organized event of the season Friday, that being a prospect camp practice. He'll play in at least one of two exhibition games against Blues prospects Monday and Tuesday before main training camp begins.</p><p>This Hawks prospect team isn't as star-studded as those of years past. So many of their <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/08/16/blackhawks-prospect-rankings-vaclav-nestrasil-sacha-boisvert-john-mustard" target="_blank" >talented young players</a> are now in the NHL and not asked to attend this camp, or in college and not allowed to attend.</p><p>A trio of likely Rockford-bound forwards in Spellacy, Sacha Boisvert and Marek Vanacker are the headliners. All three are hard-nosed players who can create havoc in dirty areas. Vanacker probably has the highest offensive upside, but Spellacy and Boisvert (who bulked up a ton this summer) are closer to NHL-ready.</p><p>"Obviously, there's an opportunity," Spellacy said. "I'll take it day-by-day, but I'll do everything I can to show myself the best and be a good teammate and use my strengths. ... I have a lot of experience from the past couple years, so I'm pretty confident going into this [camp]."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">First official Blackhawks event of the season is getting underway: Prospect camp practice <a href="https://t.co/sLhbAV0AA4">pic.twitter.com/sLhbAV0AA4</a></p>— Ben Pope (@BenPopeCST) <a href="https://x.com/BenPopeCST/status/2098427464011702685?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">September 11, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Boisvert said Spellacy stood out the most to him in practice, praising his skating and ability to get to the net. Vanacker described Spellacy as an "extremely physical" player who's "fun to battle with." Spellacy named Capitals power forward Tom Wilson as his NHL model.</p><p>Spellacy has demonstrated an ability to elevate his game when playing alongside (and against) higher-level players, including at the aforementioned <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2024/09/30/blackhawks-prospects-aj-spellacy-nhl-training-camp-windsor" target="_blank" >2024 Hawks camp</a> as well as in the 2025-26 world junior championships. It'll be interesting to see if that pattern continues as an every-day pro.</p><p>It'll also be interesting to see if he develops more of an offensive touch in the coming years. When he switched from football, he loved hitting but wasn't particularly comfortable with the puck on his stick. That was only four years ago, so perhaps he has upside in that regard that simply hasn't revealed itself yet.</p><p>"That's a huge thing. You need to be good with the puck," Spellacy said. "Obviously I can skate and play physical, but [I've worked on] making those little plays, picking up pucks off the wall, getting to the net...and being able to finish plays."</p>

entries.title: Judge to appoint receiver to take control of West Suburban, Weiss Memorial hospitals amid legal battle
entries.summary: <p>A Cook County judge has decided to appoint a receiver to take control of two safety-net hospitals whose fate has been tied up in court hearings for months.</p><p>Cook County Circuit Court Judge Patrick Stanton said at a hearing Friday that it was time for someone to take control of West Suburban Medical Center and Weiss Memorial Hospital as the hospitals’ owner, Resilience Healthcare CEO Manoj Prasad, and landlord, Rathnakar Reddy Patlola, continue their <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/05/26/west-suburban-medical-center-oak-park-prasad-patlola-resilience-healthcare" target="_blank" ><u>court battle</u></a> over a settlement agreement.</p><p>“Someone needs to take control of this, and it should no longer be the current parties,” said Stanton.</p><p>Stanton’s decision was a win for Patlola, who had <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/04/22/west-suburban-medical-center-lawsuit-receiver-ramco-resilience-healthcare" target="_blank" ><u>asked</u></a> the judge months ago to appoint a receiver to oversee the hospitals. He denied the request at the time, but several problems have since emerged that he said now make a receiver necessary.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/05/26/west-suburban-medical-center-oak-park-prasad-patlola-resilience-healthcare" >West Suburban Medical Center’s closing triggered a legal battle between its owners</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>A factor in the judge’s decision was Weiss Memorial Hospital losing its Illinois hospital license this week. The Illinois Department of Public Health terminated the hospital’s provisional license Wednesday after Resilience Healthcare failed to demonstrate that substantial improvements had been made to the hospital since it shut its doors last year.</p><p>“Despite having over a year to make improvements at Weiss Memorial, hospital leadership has not demonstrated the necessary improvements to safely re-open the hospital to care for the community’s residents,” the Illinois Department of Public Health said in a statement.</p><p>The judge said he did not want to see the same happen to West Suburban Hospital.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-030000" name="image-030000"></a> <picture entries.title: Cook County judge has sheriff’s deputies placed in custody for refusing to unshackle murder defendant
entries.summary: <p>A Cook County judge had two sheriff’s deputies detained this week for refusing to unshackle a man facing murder charges so he could embrace his family — a move the deputies’ union described as “an outrageous abuse of the court's authority.”</p><p>The incident happened Wednesday after Circuit Judge John F. Lyke Jr. invited the defendant’s relatives to step forward for a hug, according to a court transcript. When the deputies told him they needed to wait for a supervisor’s approval to remove the defendant’s handcuffs, Lyke snapped back.</p><p>"I'm giving you a direct order to step out the way,” Lyke told the deputies, according to the transcript. </p><p>“I'm taking directive from my sergeant,” one deputy replied.</p><p>“Take him into custody,” Lyke said. “Take him in the back. If I were you, I would stop talking.”</p><p>The two sheriff’s deputies were then placed into custody for contempt of court and stripped of their badges and protective equipment, according to their union, Teamsters Local 700. Lyke ordered them to apologize or face up to 90 days in jail, the union said.</p><p>They were both released after apologizing to the judge.</p><p>Sheriff’s office policy requires supervisor approval to remove handcuffs from detainees, like this defendant, who are labeled as “high risk,” according to the union.</p><p>“Punishing two deputies for doing exactly what they are trained and required to do is an outrageous abuse of the court's authority,” Teamsters Local 700 president Ramon Williams said. “The Office of the Chief Judge needs to reprimand Judge Lyke, and Lyke owes these deputies an apology.”</p><p>The sheriff’s office said the move shows Lyke has “little concern for the challenges court deputies face in their efforts to protect the safety of the court, courtroom staff, defendants and members of the public who attend these proceedings.”</p><p>It's not the first time Lyke has threatened to jail deputies for “doing their jobs,” according to the sheriff’s office. In February 2025, Lyke ordered deputies out of a jury room where a detainee was meeting with a lawyer and family members. The deputies told him they’d been ordered to stay in the room with the detainee.</p><p>Lyke replied that he “don't give a damn” what the deputy's “bosses told them to do,” according to an incident report. Lyke then threatened to escort the deputies to the back if they “didn’t step out of the damn jury room.”</p><p>“While the sheriff’s office understands that members of the judiciary have wide latitude in how they run their courtrooms, Judge Lyke’s disrespectful and inappropriate treatment of our staff is completely unacceptable,” the sheriff's office said.</p><p>During Wednesday's altercation, Lyke told the courtroom he allows contact visits from family — “just a brief hug.”</p><p>“I don't care what they are charged with,” Lyke said. “They are still presumed innocent.”</p><p>He said courtroom officers usually let new deputies know about this practice.</p><p>The office of Chief Judge Charles S. Beach II said it has reviewed this week's incident and discussed it with sheriff's office leadership to “ensure a clear understanding of applicable procedures and responsibilities.”</p><p>Earlier this year, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/04/28/chicago-john-bartholomew-john-lyke-alphanso-talley-swedish-chicago-police-shooting" target="_blank" >Lyke drew criticism</a> for having placed Alphanso Talley, a convicted felon, on electronic monitoring before Talley allegedly killed Chicago police Officer John Bartholomew and wounded another cop at Swedish Hospital.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/04/28/chicago-john-bartholomew-john-lyke-alphanso-talley-swedish-chicago-police-shooting" target="_blank" >Judge under fire for placing suspected Chicago cop killer on home monitoring before Swedish Hospital shooting</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Bears, RB D'Andre Swift agree to contract extension
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> and D'Andre Swift agreed to terms on a three-year, $33.75 million contract Friday, his agency confirmed, saving the running back from having to play this season on the last year of his deal.</p><p>The extension gives Swift guaranteed money beyond this year and helps the Bears hedge against the rising costs of running backs. Last month, the Lions' Jahmyr Gibbs, the Falcons' Bijan Robinson and the Colts' Jonathan Taylor agreed to top-of-the-market extensions. Swift's new deal settles in the middle class.</p><p>After Swift posted perhaps the most impressive training camp of any Bears player, general manger Ryan Poles didn't rule out a new deal when asked about it last week. Players and teams usually treat the first game of the year as an artificial deadline to get deals done.</p><p>"I think he's done a great job,” Poles said then. “I love his approach this offseason. He looks amazing. Second year in [Ben Johnson’s offensive] system too. ... This is where this job gets tough, trying to figure out how you want to allocate everything not only for now but into the future. We'll have those conversations and see where we want to go with it. I love Swiftie. I love the way that he's working.”</p><p>Poles has to be conscientious about how he allocates money next year and beyond. Quarterback Caleb Williams and wide receiver Rome Odunze will be eligible for contract extensions the minute this season ends, and the Bears already presume that they'll have to pay tight end Colston Loveland a lofty price a year later.</p><p>Swift spent his first three years in Detroit, where Johnson worked, before being traded to the Eagles in 2023. After pursuing Saquon Barkley, the Bears signed Swift to a three-year, $24 million deal in March 2024. Swift struggled in his first year with the Bears but was outstanding last season. With help from running backs coach Eric Bieniemy, who has since left for the Chiefs, Swift focused on staying true to the running path of each play and running for fewer losses. He averaged 4.9 yards per carry on 223 rushes last season after averaging 3.8 on 253 rushes a year earlier. He ran for a career-high nine rushing touchdowns last season.</p><p>"I think he's just put himself in position to have a great year," running backs coach Eric Studesville said Thursday. "I love how he works. He's been more impressive in person. I was already impressed with him on tape.”</p>

entries.title: Sky owner Michael Alter should reconsider one-man band approach to front office
entries.summary: <p>Principal owner Michael Alter told reporters <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/08/25/sky-ban-enes-kanter-freedom-from-games-according-to-principal-owner-michael-alter" >earlier this month</a> that he isn’t happy that the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" >Sky</a> are missing the playoffs for the third year in a row.</p><p>That should be a given.</p><p>If he’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/08/28/owner-michael-alter-is-not-happy-about-sky-missing-playoffs-again-so-what-should-he-do" >planning to do anything about it</a>, he should be paying attention to the Sparks.</p><p>Not because the Sparks are necessarily a model WNBA franchise. In fact, they’ve made many of the same mistakes as the Sky in recent years. They got caught flat-footed for the first wave of teams building practice facilities, and their reputation suffered. They’ve also <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/07/21/the-all-stars-the-sky-couldve-had-are-coming-to-chicago" >traded away lottery picks</a> who have become All-Stars for other teams, without any playoff bids to show for it.</p><p>These disappointments have left both teams in a tough spot.</p><p>But the Sparks are responding differently than the Sky.</p><p>They fired their general manager, Reagan Pebley, who came in with no front office experience, and replaced her with a longtime NBA scout and executive, Ariana Andonian.</p><p>They’ve also quietly revamped their front office to include two experienced assistant general managers, Zach Knowlton and Nate Nielsen, as well as hiring analysts to support them.</p><p>This isn’t a revolutionary move. The Lynx, Storm, Liberty and Mercury have all led the charge in professionalizing their front offices — now other teams have to match that to stay competitive.</p><p>And if the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/03/13/new-breed-of-expansion-teams-in-toronto-and-portland-to-challenge-the-sky-in-2026" >expansion teams</a>' approach is an indicator of the trend, it won’t be long before front offices in the W start to look more like their NBA counterparts: staffed by teams of scouts to evaluate talent, alongside number-crunchers who can provide analytical insights.</p><p>So what is the Sky’s plan here? General manager Jeff Pagliocca was promoted from within the organization in 2023, but still does not have an assistant GM or a dedicated team under him.</p><p>Maybe Alter’s comfortable with the one-man band, given Pagliocca’s strengths.</p><p>This past offseason, Pagliocca had some scouting wins, like finding undrafted guard Sydney Taylor, and a promising trade return in landing Rickea Jackson from the Sparks. Going forward, he should be able to leverage strong relationships around the league — former players including Kahleah Copper, Marina Mabrey, and Michaela Onyenwere have vouched for his integrity and personability to the Sun-Times.</p><p>But you don’t have to look far to see what’s missing without a numbers-oriented team behind you. Take the Lynx, one of Pagliocca’s first trade partners in 2024. The Lynx traded down in that draft to get a pick swap from the Sky in 2026. It was based on a projection that the Sky would end up a lottery team, and they were right — the Sky ultimately sent them the No. 2 pick in 2026.</p><p>The Lynx used it to draft point guard Olivia Miles, a generational talent, and sit comfortably atop the league standings.</p><p>The Lynx, of course, got lucky that Miles was available at No. 2, but that’s part of the point — smart projections can put you in a position to be lucky. Conversely, a one-man band approach can leave you vulnerable to bad luck.</p><p>As a long-time business executive, Alter should understand this.</p><p>He should also know that adding brainpower to the front office wouldn’t cost a fortune —<br>and that it’s not just about hiring people for optic's sake. It’s about having a vision for what a successful WNBA team looks like in 2026.</p><p>If Alter’s got one in mind, he needs to start showing it.</p>

entries.title: Boy gunned down in 'heartbreaking' Loop skate park attack tried to run away, police and alder say
entries.summary: <p>Detectives found a revolver, a blood trail and video footage from Metra after three assailants gunned down a South Shore boy in a skate park earlier this week in the South Loop. </p><p>Three assailants attacked Dorian D. Smith, shooting him in the neck just after 9 p.m. Wednesday in the skate park at 1135 S. Michigan Ave. before running away north to Metra train tracks, according to Chicago police reports obtained by the Sun-Times. </p><p>Smith, who apparently tried to run away in the opposite direction, was taken to Northwestern Memorial Hospital where he was pronounced dead at 9:45 p.m., the reports said. An autopsy determined Smith, of the South Shore neighborhood, died of a gunshot wound to the neck and his death was ruled a homicide, according to the Cook County medical examiner's office. </p><p>Officers who responded to a call of shots fired found blood droplets trailing in a southeast direction across the skate park leading to a pool of blood, according to the reports. </p><p>No shell casings were located on scene but a revolver, which does not expel shell casings, was found on a Metra platform, according to the reports. </p><p>Smith was a CPS student at Art in Motion, a charter school, according to the report. The school did not respond to requests for comment. </p><p>In a statement released Friday, Lamont J. Robinson (4th) condemned the "heartbreaking" attack, which was "deeply unsettling" for residents and also for the many bystanders attending a Chicago Fire game at Soldier Field, which began about 8:30 p.m. </p><p>"There are no adequate words for a family having to bury a 16-year-old, someone who should have had his whole life ahead of him, now taken by gun violence," Robinson said in the statement. "My deepest condolences go to this young man's family, his friends, and everyone who knew and loved him."</p><p>"As Vice Chair of the Police and Fire Committee, I condemn this reckless act of gun violence," Robinson said in the statement. "We owe this family answers, and we owe our community action. We need to find whoever is responsible and hold them accountable."</p><p>"We will continue working with CPD, the Park District, and our community partners to make sure our public spaces are safe, and to do everything we can to prevent another family from experiencing this kind of heartbreak," Robinson said in the statement. </p><p>"I urge anyone who witnessed what happened or has information to come forward and help detectives," the statement concluded. </p><p>Area 3 detectives are investigating. </p><p>No arrests have been made. <br></p>
