entries.title: The Big Ten is in for a rough Saturday — and many folks will be glad to see it
entries.summary: <p>It’s the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/college-sports" target="_blank" >Big Ten</a>’s world. Everybody else is just living in it.</p><p>That’s the kind of boasting a conference can do when it has steamrolled to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/college-sports/2026/09/02/big-ten-football-preview-ohio-state-oregon-indiana-michigan-illinois-northwestern-cfb" target="_blank" >back-to-back-to-back national championships</a>, with three different members combining to do the honors.</p><p>“This is the best league in the country,” every Big Ten coach has said at least 37 times already this season.</p><p>So why do I smell a Saturday comeuppance coming?</p><p>On the main stage: <b>No. 1 Ohio State (+1½) at No. 4 Texas </b>(6:30 p.m., ABC 7) in college football’s nonconference game of the year. It gets no bigger than this.</p><p>But there’s also a vast army of riled-up football watchers who are waving torches and jabbing pitchforks in the direction of Ann Arbor, Michigan, where <b>No. 11 Oklahoma (-5½) at Michigan </b>(11 a.m., Fox 32) is sure to steal some of the Buckeyes’ and Longhorns’ thunder. Why? Because so many want to see the Wolverines go down — hard — after their travesty of a 13-12 victory over major underdog Western Michigan in Week 1.</p><p>Most of you know what happened: The Wolverines ran out of time against Western Michigan, with three zeroes on the scoreboard clock before what seemed to be the final play concluded. But then? Aha! Big Ten replay officials dug under their seat cushions and found, in miraculous and extraordinarily controversial fashion, an extra second for the Maize and Blue to run one last play. That play turned into a 47-yard walk-off Hail Mary from Bryce Underwood to JJ Buchanan.</p><p>A mega-upset was averted. Fairness was launched into the sun. A nation was outraged. A world was flipped on its axis. And so on.</p><p>So, yeah, if the Sooners would kindly rough up their hosts, a lot of folks would appreciate it. And if the Buckeyes happen to get dragged down, too, there won’t be many tears shed for a conference whose power and influence in sports is greater than ever but whose handling of last weekend’s fiasco left a lot to be desired.</p><p>There’s real invective toward the Big Ten at the moment, and I get it. Even if there weren’t, though, the Wolverines and the Buckeyes would be in serious danger.</p><p>Oklahoma, coming off a 51-0 win against UTEP, is a huge step up in competition from Western Michigan, which could well be the best team in the MAC. Is Underwood really ready to put an awful Week 1 performance behind him against this Sooners defense? Especially considering his coach, Kyle Whittingham, doesn’t seem to have much confidence in it himself?</p><p>“He’s our QB right now,” Whittingham said. “It’s not something that’s infinite. At some point, we’ve got to turn the corner and we’ve got to see improvement.”</p><p>Boomer Sooner is my call, 24-17.</p><p>And the Buckeyes? They beat Texas 14-7 last year in Columbus, Ohio, pretty much blowing the lid off Longhorns quarterback Arch Manning’s Heisman Trophy chances in the season opener. The season before that, they got the better of Texas in the playoff en route to the title. They surely are confident going into this one.</p><p>It will be a glorious display of talent on the field in Austin, especially at the wide receiver position; these likely are the strongest two receiver units in the country. OSU’s Jeremiah Smith could be the NFL’s next No. 1 overall draft pick, and Texas’ Cam Coleman is widely projected to be among the top handful of picks himself. Manning, seemingly headed toward becoming the first QB drafted, has put last year’s rough start deep in the rear-view. Not to be overlooked is Longhorns edge rusher Colin Simmons, who had 21 sacks over the last two seasons and projects as yet another top-10 pick.</p><p>Simmons is a monster. His team is a monster. Hook ’Em gets it done, 23-20, and the Big Ten is left licking its wounds.</p><h3><b>OTHER WEEK 2 PICKS</b></h3><p><i>All games are Saturday.</i></p><p><b>Rice (+44½) at No. 3 Notre Dame </b>(2:30 p.m., NBC 5, 780-AM): There are 138 FBS teams, and the Owls might be right around 138th-best at throwing the football. They did rush for a whopping 458 yards in their opening win against FCS bottom-feeder Houston Christian, for whatever that’s worth. Irish, 56-3.</p><p><b>Duke (+5½) at Illinois </b>(2:30 p.m., FS1, 890-AM): By no means is this a free meal for the Illini against the defending ACC champs. Last year at Duke, though, the Illini survived an even first half before leaning on the Blue Devils like a bigger, more physical team should, wearing them down and winning 45-19; it was the epitome of what Bret Bielema wants his teams to look like. This won’t be that easy, because the Blue Devils are no slouches. They sacked Luke Altmyer four times last year, and it would have been more against a less-experienced QB. New starter Katin Houser has to be crafty. Give me the Block I, 31-24.</p><p><b>No. 12 Alabama (-10½) at Kentucky </b>(2:30 p.m., ABC 7): New Kentucky coach Will Stein has ripped a page out of the playbook of Indiana’s Curt Cignetti by bragging about how good he is. Got to respect his rhetorical game. In other news, Roll Tide, 34-20.</p><p>My favorite favorite: <b>No. 21 Iowa (-13½) vs. Iowa State </b>(6:30 p.m., NBC 5): Yes, it’s an unpredictable rivalry. But former Cyclones coach Matt Campbell took a ton of his best players with him to Penn State, setting up what should be a blip in the close-game department.</p><p>My favorite underdog: <b>Minnesota (+1½) vs. Mississippi State </b>(2:30 p.m., CBS 2): The Bulldogs are a lower-half SEC team, of which there is no doubt. The Gophers might not be an upper-half Big Ten team, but home turf matters a lot.</p><p><b>Last week: </b>6-1 straight-up, 3-4 against the spread.</p><p><b>Season to date: </b>6-1 straight-up, 3-4 against the spread.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/college-sports/2026/09/02/big-ten-football-preview-ohio-state-oregon-indiana-michigan-illinois-northwestern-cfb" >Big Ten football preview: Ohio State, Oregon or Indiana at the top? Where do Illinois, Northwestern come in?</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/college-sports/2026/08/28/chicago-state-university-football-northeast-conference-bobby-rome-fcs-cfb" target="_blank" >At Chicago State University, football is a whole new ballgame</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="113" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/0DA6p_NbVWg?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="#11 Illinois vs Duke Highlights | Week 2 | 2025 College Football Highlights"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p></p>

entries.title: Bears practice and injury report: Is WR Rome Odunze in or out vs. Panthers on Sunday?
entries.summary: <p>Breaking down <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >the Bears</a>’ Friday practice at Halas Hall:</p><h3><b>Odunze playing</b></h3><p>The Bears listed wide receiver Rome Odunze as questionable because of a strained right calf he suffered last week, but he shot through the smoke and said he’s good to go. “I’m feeling ready to go; I doubt I’m questionable,” he said with a smile. “I plan on playing.” He missed five games last season because of a stress fracture in his foot and finished with 44 catches, 661 yards and six touchdowns.</p><h3><b>Bagent iffy</b></h3><p>Bears coach Ben Johnson was tightlipped about backup quarterback Tyson Bagent, who hurt his back in practice Tuesday and has been out since. The Bears listed him as questionable, and without him, they’d go with 38-year-old journeyman Case Keenum as the backup to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/09/11/as-engineer-and-artist-blend-styles-bears-ben-johnson-gets-goosebumps-about-future-with-caleb-williams" >Caleb Williams</a>. Keenum last played in 2023.</p><h3><b>Woods returns</b></h3><p>Starting safety Xavier Woods was back on the field Friday missing part of practice Thursday with a groin injury, signaling he’ll likely play despite being listed as questionable.</p><h3><b>Trapilo available?</b></h3><h3></h3><p>It's unlikely the Bears will play left tackle Ozzy Trapilo this early as he recovers from a major knee injury, but they listed him as questionable for the game. Braxton Jones will start.</p><h3><b>Play the hits</b></h3><p>There’d been a lot of North Carolina-themed music at practice this week, but Friday the Bears stretched to Drake’s “Ran to Atlanta.” That song has a refrain that repeats, “Iceman turnt,” which might’ve made the playlist as a nod to Williams.</p>
entries.author: Jason Lieser

entries.title: Bears coach Ben Johnson's encore starts in his home state
entries.summary: <p>As a tribute to their <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/09/11/as-engineer-and-artist-blend-styles-bears-ben-johnson-gets-goosebumps-about-future-with-caleb-williams" target="_blank" >North Carolinian head coach</a> — and a nod to the Panthers, their Week 1 opponent Sunday — the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> started every practice this week by blaring songs about the Carolinas on their speaker system.</p><p>There was the classic: James Taylor’s “Carolina on My Mind.”</p><p>There was a cover of “Wagon Wheel” by Darius Rucker, who hails from South Carolina.</p><p>And then there was Ben Johnson’s favorite, “Raise Up” by the North Carolina rapper Petey Pablo. It was released in 2001 — when Johnson was 15 — and was certified as a gold record. In the song, the rapper screams the name of his home state and encourages the listener to “take off your shirt, twist it around your hand and spin it like a helicopter.”</p><p>The Bears coach remembers playing the song at his wedding reception. Johnson, notorious for taking his shirt off after the Bears’ “Black Friday” win in Philadelphia last year, was quick to say that, no, he did not follow the song’s instructions then.</p><p>“Shirt stayed on,” he said with a smile Friday.</p><p>Johnson is starting his second season with the Bears by playing in his home state Sunday. Expectations are sky-high for Johnson, who last year took a 5-12 team with a fledgling quarterback and made it into a 11-6 NFC North champion. He led the Bears to their first playoff win in 15 years, managed to pick a fight with the Packers’ head coach and seemingly put quarterback Caleb Williams back on track toward becoming a fixture for the next decade.</p><p>Whatever he does for an encore, it will start in North Carolina.</p><p>Sunday marks his fourth game ever at Bank of America Stadium. The first three went poorly, with Johnson’s Lions losing to the Panthers twice by a combined 34 points in 2022 and 2020 and his Dolphins losing by 24 in 2012. This time, though, is special — he’s the head coach. His wife Jessica, whom he met in grade school, has peppered the head coach with the things she plans to do back in North Carolina. Both his family and hers will make the two-hour drive from the mountains of Asheville, where they grew up, to Charlotte for the weekend.</p><p>“I think it probably means more to my wife than it does myself, to be honest with you,” Johnson said. “She’s made some comments — and I'm like, ‘Giiiiirl, you do whatever you want to do. I’m good.’”</p><p>Taylor went to Carolina in his mind. Johnson, though, will remain inside his own mind even as his family — and team — come in for the game. This is a work trip, after all.</p><p>Johnson is never more busy — or intense — than he is the 24 hours before kickoff. He has meetings throughout Saturday while he whittles down the team’s game plan as the offensive play-caller. On Sunday mornings, he gets to the stadium early and locks himself in his office to make his final preparations.</p><p>“We certainly have the plays to bed at that point in terms of what we want on the plan,” he said, “and yet, the timing of those plays sometimes doesn’t get determined until the morning of.”</p><p>He’s focused — and emotionally distant — until kickoff. His own assistants know to steer clear.</p><p>“I feel a responsibility to those guys, to the coaching staff and to those players — I don’t want to let them down,” Johnson said. “Everybody’s different. It just so happens for me to make sure I’m at my best, I don’t like being distracted in any way, shape or form. …</p><p>“It’s my process of what gets me right for game day. ”</p><p>A quarterback from grade school through college — he walked on at North Carolina — Johnson loved the Panthers’ Jake Delhomme as a kid. He admired two Panthers stars who eventually played for the Bears, edge rusher Julius Peppers and receiver Muhsin Muhammad.</p><p>After a state title-winning stint at A.C. Reynolds High School in Asheville, Johnson walked on to play quarterback at North Carolina in 2004. He was listed as an “athlete” — and not a quarterback — his first year, though, and the team issued him No. 23.</p><p>That number is sacred, both in Chapel Hill and Chicago — it’s what Michael Jordan wore with the Tar Heels and Bulls.</p><p>"Everybody wore that number to the game,” Johnson said with a smile.</p><p>He was switched to No. 14 for his last three years. When he left UNC, Johnson got a job as a graduate assistant at Boston College, where he worked with linebacker Luke Kuechly. He was drafted in the first round by the Panthers and this summer was inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame. It gave Johnson another reason to follow the team from his home state — one he's been unable to beat on their soil.</p><p>“Yeah,” Johnson said, “I got a lot of favorites there.”</p>
entries.author: Patrick Finley

entries.title: Illinois alerts more than 700,000 people they will or could lose public health insurance
entries.summary: <p>The Pritzker administration is alerting more than 700,000 people across Illinois that they will lose, or are at risk of losing, their public health insurance due to unprecedented changes from the federal government.</p><p>Officials estimate about half of these enrollees live in Cook County.</p><p>The state has <a class="Link" href="https://hfs.illinois.gov/content/dam/soi/en/web/hfs/medicalclients/medicaidguide/ACAAdultCustomerNotice083126ToPrint.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>mailed letters</u></a> to people who have Medicaid public health insurance, a state-federal program for those who are low-income or have disabilities. About 3 million people have Medicaid coverage in Illinois, around 1 in 4 people.</p><p>“It could be a huge step backwards,” said Kathy Chan, director of policy at Cook County Health in Chicago, one of the largest public health systems in the U.S. “We and many other partners … are working towards a goal of trying to mitigate the harm as much as we can, and try to preserve coverage for as many people who are still eligible as possible.”</p><p>The significant <a class="Link" href="https://hfs.illinois.gov/medicalclients/medicaidguide/changes.html" target="_blank" ><u>changes are coming</u></a> due to H.R. 1, known as the <a class="Link" href="https://www.kff.org/medicaid/medicaid-work-requirements-tracker-overview/" target="_blank" ><u>One Big Beautiful Bill</u></a>, that President Trump signed into law last year.</p><p>They <a class="Link" href="https://hfs.illinois.gov/medicalclients/medicaidguide/changes.html" target="_blank" ><u>affect mostly two groups</u></a> of people who have Medicaid statewide.</p><p>Starting Oct. 1, about 8,500 people who are not U.S. citizens but have legal status,<a class="Link" href="https://hfs.illinois.gov/content/dam/soi/en/web/hfs/medicalclients/hbia_hbis/cn2628hrinocenglish07242026.pdf" target="_blank" ><u> such as refugees and survivors of trafficking, will lose coverage</u></a>. H.R. 1 narrows which immigrants qualify for Medicaid.</p><p>Next year, about 700,000 people who have joined Medicaid since Illinois expanded eligibility under the Affordable Care Act <a class="Link" href="https://www.civicfed.org/iifs/blog/governor-signs-bill-expand-medicaid-illinois" target="_blank" ><u>more than a decade ago</u></a> are at risk of losing coverage. That’s if they don’t meet work or volunteer requirements. And they will need to prove they are eligible every six months, instead of just once a year.</p><p>This group is known as “ACA adults.” They are 19 to 64 years old. They don’t have children younger than 18 at home.</p><p>These adults must work or volunteer at least 80 hours a month — about four hours a day Monday through Friday — or they could be in school at least part-time, among other criteria. A person could also do a combination of work, volunteer and school to meet requirements, according to the state.</p><p>ACA adults who are new to Medicaid as of Jan. 1 would need to comply immediately.</p><p>For current enrollees who don’t comply, the earliest they would lose coverage is April 1, according to a spokesperson for the Illinois Department of Healthcare and Family Services, which oversees Medicaid. More people could lose their insurance on a rolling basis depending on whether they meet the new work requirements when it’s time to renew their coverage.</p><p>There are <a class="Link" href="https://hfs.illinois.gov/content/dam/soi/en/web/hfs/medicalclients/medicaidguide/ACAAdultCustomerNotice083126ToPrint.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>several exemptions</u></a> for ACA adults, including if a Medicaid enrollee is pregnant or postpartum, if they’re a parent, guardian or caregiver of a child younger than 14 or if they are “medically frail.” That’s broadly defined as having a substance use or serious mental health condition, or a serious or complex medical condition that requires regular treatment, among other factors.</p><p>One of the most daunting tasks: spreading the word to Medicaid recipients that big changes are coming and making sure they get paperwork to the state on time so they don’t become uninsured. That could have <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/health-medicine/2026/07/31/cook-county-predicts-charity-care-will-soar-to-highest-level-in-more-than-a-decade-medicaid-obamacare" target="_blank" ><u>far-reaching ripple effects</u></a> on hospitals, clinics and even for people who have commercial insurance, local leaders have warned.</p><p>HFS declined an interview request but responded to questions over email and shared letters the agency sent to Medicaid enrollees.</p><p>Even for Medicaid enrollees who aren’t subject to the new rules, there will likely be more confusion heading into 2027, Chan said. Medicaid is a complicated program, and every month about 10 to 15 percent of enrollees lose coverage not because they aren’t eligible, but because of some hiccup with the paperwork getting to them, or getting back to the state, Chan said.</p><p>For example, not everyone has a steady mailing address, or might have trouble navigating the online system, Chan said. Cook County and other organizations have created an <a class="Link" href="https://getmedicaidfacts.com/" target="_blank" ><u>online tool kit</u></a> to help Medicaid enrollees navigate these changes.</p><p>Jessica Davenport-Williams, co-founder of Black Girls Break Bread, an advocacy organization that works to reduce barriers to medical care for women and children in particular, is especially worried that pregnant and postpartum mothers could fall through the cracks.</p><p>She wonders, who will tell the state that a woman with a Medicaid plan is pregnant to make sure she’s exempt from work requirements, when it can take months to get a doctor’s appointment, or she isn’t connected to a doctor and plans to give birth at home? Otherwise, she risks becoming uninsured.</p><p>In Illinois, about <a class="Link" href="https://dph.illinois.gov/content/dam/soi/en/web/idph/publications/idph/topics-and-services/life-stages-populations/maternal-child-family-health-services/maternal-health/maternal-mortality-data-report-2025.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>one-third of pregnancy-related deaths</u></a> happen more than 60 days after a woman has her baby, according to the state public health department.</p><p>“Access to care is very important, especially with our maternal health deserts,” Davenport-Williams said.</p><p><i>Kristen Schorsch is a senior reporter covering public health for WBEZ.</i></p>

entries.title: City poised to spend $14M more in settlements linked to disgraced ex-Chicago police detective
entries.summary: <p>Chicago taxpayers may have to spend another nearly $14 million to compensate two defendants framed for murders by corrupt Chicago Police Detective Reynaldo Guevara.</p><p>The settlements will come before the City Council's finance committee on Monday, along with a $6 million payout to the family of a man killed after another police chase gone wrong.</p><p>Forty-three people, including three women, have been exonerated after they were sent to prison on murder convictions in cases handled by Guevara in the 1980s and 1990s. Most of them lived in Humboldt Park.</p><p>As of last winter, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/02/07/wrongful-convictions-burge-guevara-watts-chicago" target="_blank" ><u>lawsuits targeting him</u></a> already cost the city and county at least $80 million. In February, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/02/09/det-reynaldo-guevara-settlements-chicago-police-department-misconduct" target="_blank" ><u>City Council approved another $29.2 million</u></a> linked to allegations of his police misconduct.</p><p>At the time, the law department recommended approval of the Guevara-related settlements, saying they would “reduce financial exposure and bring the matters to a responsible close.”</p><p>Last year, Mayor Brandon Johnson came under fire for borrowing money, to be repaid over five years, to bankroll a<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2025/09/25/city-council-approval-90m-settlement-chicago-police-department-ronald-watts" target="_blank" ><u> $90 million global settlement </u></a>that put to rest 176 lawsuits tied to former Chicago police Sgt. Ronald Watts, who was accused of framing hundreds of people on drug charges at the Chicago Housing Authority's Ida B. Wells complex.</p><p>The two new settlements are expected to turn up the heat on city Corporation Counsel Mary<i> </i>Richardson-Lowry to strike a similar global settlement, resolving dozens of remaining Guevara cases.</p><p>In 1998, Mariano and Jacinta Soto were stabbed to death in their home and their two children — a 2-month-old daughter and a 3-year old son — were kidnapped. </p><p>Gabriel Solache and Arturo DeLeon-Reyes said they falsely confessed to the gruesome crimes after they were interrogated for over 40 hours, beaten by Guevara, and deprived of food and water. </p><p>The day of the killing, Adriana Mejia, who lived in the same building as Solache and DeLeon-Reyes, told her husband she’d given birth to a child and had agreed to watch another woman’s son whom she’d met at the hospital. A week later, a relative saw the news of the Soto murders and recognized the children from Mejia’s home. Solache and DeLeon-Reyes accompanied the woman’s husband to bring the boy to the police station, at his request. DeLeon-Reyes was sentenced to life in prison and Solache was sentenced to death. Each man spent nearly 20 years in prison before their charges were dismissed.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/09/03/mayor-brandon-johnson-2027-budget-forecast-chicago-city-hall-deficit" target="_blank" ><u>Johnson is facing an $882.4 million shortfall next year,</u></a> driven in part by the mountain of legal settlements. The city is attempting to reject the full cost of legal settlements for police misconduct instead of deliberately underestimating the payouts, only to pay double and triple that amount.</p><p>This time, officials are estimating $400 million for 2027 settlements, calling that new projection the “largest driver” of the city's increased costs.</p><p>“We want to be very transparent about the cost of these settlements and judgments that are related to actions that occurred decades ago,” said acting Budget Director Jonathan Ernst.</p><p>The $6 million settlement of another errant police chase goes to the family of Michael Jordan. </p><p>The father of three was struck by a driver being chased by Chicago police while sitting at a CTA bus shelter near 99th Street and Van Vlissingen Road in June 2019. </p><p>When officers attempted to stop a Jeep that had been reported stolen, the driver speeded off and crashed into the shelter just seconds later.</p>
entries.author: Fran Spielman

entries.title: Amid pitching issues, Alex Bregman, Cubs show what bats are capable of: ‘Being the best offense in baseball’
entries.summary: <p>After <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/09/cubs-kevin-gausman-trade-deadline-jed-hoyer-brewers-starting-rotation-playoff-starter-clay-holmes-ian-happ-phil-maton" >being swept by the division-dominating Brewers</a> earlier this week, there’s panic across the North Side.</p><p>And it’s not unwarranted, with the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> tumbling from their onetime perch atop the NL wild-card standings to the thick of the race, sparking <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/10/cubs-brewers-nl-central-standings-nl-wild-card-standings-phillies-diamondbacks-padres-playoffs-postseason-kevin-gausman-craig-counsell-ian-happ" >a late-season fight for a playoff spot</a>.</p><p>But while it took a lot going wrong to force another downturn in what’s been a roller-coaster season, the Cubs spent Friday delivering a reminder of what could still go very, very right.</p><p>The bats exploded for 16 hits and a dozen runs in a 12-2 blowout win over the Pirates, the highest-scoring team in baseball showing what it’s capable of if it can secure that ticket to the postseason.</p><p>“It’s capable of being the best offense in baseball,” third baseman <b>Alex Bregman</b> said after the victory, which stopped a four-game losing streak. “We’ve shown that this year. We’ve just got to be consistent with what we’re doing.”</p><p>Consistency is undoubtedly key, the thing that the pitching staff has lacked during a bumpy back half of August and first couple weeks in September.</p><p>Bregman — who slumped so badly during his opening months in a Cubs uniform that he was getting booed at Wrigley Field — has been <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/21/cubs-alex-bregman-playoffs-stats-world-series-dansby-swanson-carson-kelly-craig-counsell" >a model of that consistency since the All-Star break</a>.</p><p>He hit his 25th homer and his 30th double as part of a three-hit day Friday, and the questions about the front office’s big spend on him last offseason are all but forgotten.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Alex Bregman clubs his 25th homer of the season 💪 <a href="https://t.co/Vm5STCMP7z">pic.twitter.com/Vm5STCMP7z</a></p>— MLB (@MLB) <a href="https://x.com/MLB/status/2098498254283391319?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">September 11, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Alongside MVP candidate <b>Pete Crow-Armstrong</b>, Bregman looks capable of carrying this team in October, a month he knows well, having played more than 100 postseason games in his career and winning a pair of World Series rings with the Astros.</p><p>After hitting .235 with seven home runs and 14 doubles in his first 92 games this season, Bregman is batting .310 with 18 homers and 16 doubles in the 53 games since.</p><p>“Probably like June, I just decided I don’t really care what my numbers look like, I care about fixing my mechanics for the rest of my career,” Bregman said of his midseason turnaround. “That mentality allows you not to chase hitting seven homers in one at-bat. It allows you just to take one at-bat at a time and win the next pitch and win the next at-bat.</p><p>“I’ve stuck to that, for the most part. It’s hard. It’s tempting to go up there and try to get it all back with one swing.”</p><p>The Cubs still need to show a lot more on the pitching side of things, coming into Friday with, by one statistical measure, the worst staff in baseball; they ranked 30 out of 30 with 3.7 fWAR as a group.</p><p>But the bats were on the other side of the spectrum, leading baseball with 34.4 fWAR, a sign, just like Friday’s performance, of what’s still possible.</p><h3><b>Swanson back soon</b></h3><p>Shortstop <b>Dansby Swanson</b> is nearing his return from an oblique strain that’s sidelined him since the middle of August.</p><p>Swanson will begin a minor league rehab assignment with Triple-A Iowa next week, with the Cubs hoping to bring their shortstop off the injured list for next weekend’s series against the Reds in Cincinnati.</p><h3><b>Cabrera, too?</b></h3><p>The Cubs are also nearing a decision on right-hander <b>Edward Cabrera</b> and a return to the big league team.</p><p>The results haven’t been pretty in a trio of minor league outings — he’s allowed six runs in 3⅔ innings — but he’s healthy after battling the latest round of blister troubles. The Cubs could certainly use help in their beleaguered bullpen.</p>
entries.author: Vinnie Duber

entries.title: Clay Holmes focused on winning with Cubs this year, but trade acquisition could make nice future piece
entries.summary: <p>Clay Holmes can feel it in the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a>’ clubhouse.</p><p>This team wants to win.</p><p>“It’s been a very easy transition for me,” the Cubs righty said Wednesday. “Everything’s about winning. You’re in that competitive environment, and you get to focus on and do the things that you want to do. It makes showing up to work a lot of fun every day.”</p><p>A ringing endorsement for a team that could benefit from Holmes being more than just a two-month rental.</p><p>The Cubs hope that Holmes ends up at the very least a three-month rental, his stay — and their season — extending to the end of October. That’s why Jed Hoyer’s front office <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/03/cubs-mlb-trade-deadline-jed-hoyer-top-prospects-trades-kevin-gausman-clay-holmes-ryan-zeferjahn-braxton-garrett-tyrone-taylor" >made an aggressive move at the deadline</a>, parting with No. 2 prospect Jefferson Rojas to pry Holmes from the Mets.</p><p>Holmes has, for the most part, performed as the top-of-the-rotation arm Hoyer envisioned him being, allowing just one run over a four-start stretch that had him looking like a Game 1 playoff starter.</p><p>Holmes, though, has also been part of the team’s starting-pitching inconsistency, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/01/cubs-home-runs-record-jed-hoyer-front-office-pitching-starting-rotation-playoffs-postseason-shota-imanaga-matthew-boyd" >something Hoyer recently lamented</a> and something that’s reared its ugly head as the Cubs have slipped into a late-season fight for a playoff spot. Holmes <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/06/cubs-pete-crow-armstrong-40-home-runs-franchise-record-sammy-sosa-clay-holmes-ian-happ-knee-injury" >gave up a career-worst eight runs</a> his last time out against the Marlins.</p><p>But despite <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/10/cubs-brewers-nl-central-standings-nl-wild-card-standings-phillies-diamondbacks-padres-playoffs-postseason-kevin-gausman-craig-counsell-ian-happ" >slipping from the top of the NL wild-card race to the thick of it</a>, these Cubs still have eyes on the championship goals they had at the start of the season.</p><p>“There’s a lot of guys here that have signed here for a number of years, they expect to win here. They expect to win a championship here. You feel that, a lot of guys that want to win,” Holmes said. “You’re not too far removed, especially this year, from seeing the 2016 team come back, and people feel that and know how special it is for Chicago and the fans here.</p><p>“Players want to feel that, but more importantly, you want to experience that with the city again. You feel that in the locker room.”</p><p>Though the focus is on the Cubs’ suddenly murky fate, could Holmes, due for free agency at season’s end, be one of the next guys to sign with championship dreams?</p><p>From a performance standpoint, you’d have to imagine the Cubs would be interested. After all, they acquired him as an ideal partner for their best-in-baseball defense. Holmes is a ground-ball pitcher, and the Cubs count three Gold Glovers on their infield in second baseman Nico Hoerner, shortstop Dansby Swanson and third baseman Alex Bregman, all of whom are signed to long-term deals.</p><p>Holmes, who has flourished since switching from All-Star reliever to high-performing starter, would also fill what’s shaping up to be a huge need for the Cubs in 2027: starting pitching.</p><p>The entirety of their current rotation —0 Holmes, fellow righty Kevin Gausman and lefties Matthew Boyd, Shota Imanaga and David Peterson — <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/20/cade-townsend-is-cubs-pitchings-far-future-but-whats-near-future-look-like-when-starters-hit-free-agency" >is slated to hit free agency</a>.</p><p>While they could construct an intriguing starting five with guys currently in house – righties Cade Horton, Ben Brown, Edward Cabrera and Javier Assad, plus lefty Justin Steele — much of that intrigue comes from the fact that almost all of them will be coming off 2026 seasons defined by injuries, including several significant ones.</p><p>In other words, Holmes could provide an awful lot of certainty for a rotation that could be woefully short on it.</p><p>But that’s for the Cubs to worry about once the curtains come down on the 2026 season.</p><p>The next two weeks will be a fight for their playoff lives.</p><p>“When the lights get brighter and the games become more meaningful, the rest of everything else kind of drowns out. From my experience, that’s what you crave,” Holmes said. “It’s a drug. It’s all you want is just to care about this one game in front of you, and that’s all that matters.</p><p>“It’s not easy, either. You get knocked down, you have to get up. It feels like you’re a million miles away, then all of a sudden, you do a few things, and it feels like you’re on top of the mountain. It can become a roller coaster, just because of how much things mean down the stretch here.”</p>
entries.author: Vinnie Duber
